title: Jet lag in children: helping them adjust to a new time zone
description: Jet lag in children and babies: how to shift sleep and meal times, use light and make the journey calmer, with cautious, practical advice for families.
h1: Jet lag in children and babies: how to cope without stress
intro: Jet lag in children is the same mismatch between body clock and local time that you feel, but it shows more because little ones have stricter rhythms and less ability to compensate. There is no magic formula: regular routines, light at the right moment and a little patience all work. For any supplement or medicine, your paediatrician is always the reference.

paragraphs: A child has very structured sleep, meal and nap times. When local time changes suddenly, their body keeps asking for sleep and food at home time. The result is night waking, afternoon tantrums and hunger at the wrong moments.

In newborns, especially in the first months, the day-night rhythm is still forming. For them the time zone matters less as a concept, but the change of environment and routine can still make nights irregular. In this case the realistic aim is not perfection, but gradually returning to a recognisable routine.

If the time difference is a few hours and your child has a stable routine, you can shift sleep and wake-up times by about 1 hour a day in the 1-3 days before you leave. Heading east, move earlier; heading west, move later. For small shifts, or if the routine is already hard going, you can also choose not to do it and concentrate on the arrival.
With the Sfuso calculator you can see how many hours the time changes by and choose whether to leave already on shifted times or to adjust on the spot.
list: Keep the usual sleep objects: soft toy, blanket, sleeping bag.
Bring snacks and a simple meal, so you do not depend on the airline’s meal times.
If you can, choose flights that arrive at a time when your child can stay awake until the evening.

sections.h2: On the flight and on arrival
paragraphs: If the flight is overnight, let your child sleep when they are tired and do not wake them on purpose. Equally, avoid letting them skip rest altogether and arrive exhausted. On arrival, spend time outdoors: daylight is the strongest signal for helping the body clock to shift.

Usually it takes about 1 day per hour of time difference to recover if you do nothing, but with light and regular routines it gets shorter. Avoid long naps: a short rest, before mid-afternoon, may be enough to get to the evening without collapsing at 5pm.

Keep the bedtime routine identical to home: bath, story, low lights. The times change, not the gestures. If your child wakes in the middle of the night ready to play, keep the room dark and the atmosphere calm, with no screens or lively games.

In the morning open the curtains and windows and take your child outside as soon as possible. Offer meals at local times, even if they are not very hungry: hunger rhythms follow sleep rhythms and they line up together. Do not give melatonin or other supplements on your own initiative: ask your paediatrician first.

A few days of irritability, broken sleep and irregular appetite is normal. But if your child has a fever, vomiting, pain or an unwellness that does not go away, the cause may not be the time zone: in that case contact your paediatrician or a local doctor.

Remember too that you are their reference point. If you stay calm and keep to the routine, it is easier for them to find their balance. Avoid changing too many things at once and accept that the first nights will not be perfect: they usually improve within a few days.

faq.q: How long does jet lag last in children?
faq.a: It depends on the number of time zones and the direction of travel, but as a general estimate children recover in about 1 day per hour of time difference if you do nothing. Regular routines and plenty of natural daylight during the day help to shorten it. Every child is different, so be patient.

faq.q: Can I give my child melatonin for jet lag?
faq.a: Do not give it on your own initiative. Rules on melatonin vary from country to country, and for children you need your paediatrician’s opinion, who will consider age, reason and whether it is appropriate. For many little ones, natural light, regular routines and a bedtime routine identical to home are enough.

faq.q: Is it worth shifting my child’s routine before we leave?
faq.a: If the time difference is large and the routine is stable, you can shift sleep and wake-up times by about 1 hour a day in the 1-3 days before the trip. If the change is small or the child is very young, it is often simpler to adjust straight away on arrival.

title: Overnight flights and jet lag: sleep well and arrive rested
description: How to handle overnight (red-eye) flights: sleeping on board, choosing the right time, avoiding coffee and screens, and arriving with minimal jet lag.
h1: Overnight flights: how to sleep on board and limit jet lag
intro: An overnight flight, also called a red-eye, is a flight that takes off in the evening and lands the next morning, and it is best handled as a night’s sleep to protect. Jet lag depends on the time zones you cross, but the quality of your sleep on board decides how you feel on arrival. With a few practical choices you can sleep more and arrive less tired.

sections.h2: Understanding what happens to your body
paragraphs: Your lowest body temperature falls about 2 hours before you usually wake up: it is the moment when your body most wants to sleep. If your night on the plane straddles that point, your sleep will be deeper. If instead the flight takes you east, dawn arrives early and the hours of darkness get shorter.

For example, leaving the UK for New York (5 hours behind in winter), local time stays behind: there a daytime flight is more common. Heading east, like Dubai (+4), an evening flight makes you arrive when it is still the middle of the night for your body.

Arrive at the airport already rested. If the flight leaves late, do not turn up at the end of an exhausting day. Have a light meal, and avoid alcohol and have your last coffee at least 6 hours before you want to fall asleep.
If you can, choose a seat you can lean against: the window for your head, or the aisle if you get up often. Set your watch to the destination time zone and start thinking in that time.
list: Bring an eye mask and earplugs or noise-cancelling headphones.
Pack something warm: it is often cool on board.
Download a programme or relaxing music, with no bright screens before sleeping.

paragraphs: Try to fall asleep as soon as possible after the meal, without waiting for the last service. The longer and more continuous your sleep, the better. Avoid bright screens in the hour before: the blue light of your phone is exactly the signal that tells your brain to stay awake.

If the flight is short and the night reduced, broken sleep is normal. Do not force it: resting in the dark with your eyes closed helps anyway. If your landing time coincides with the local morning, resist the temptation to keep sleeping until late.

As soon as you arrive, go outdoors and seek natural light. If you land in the morning, light helps you delay your body clock heading west; heading east it helps if it comes after your temperature minimum. If you really must rest, take a nap of 20-30 minutes, never after 4pm local time.
Then stay awake until a reasonable time in the evening. The Sfuso calculator shows you, based on your wake-up time and the time difference, when to seek light and when to avoid it in the first days.

sections.h2: When an overnight flight makes sense
paragraphs: An overnight flight makes sense if it saves you a working day or if you land in the morning with the whole day ahead. Heading west it works well: you land and can stay outdoors until the evening, helping your body to delay. Heading east, instead, sleep on the plane is shorter and the arrival falls when it is still night for you.

If you can choose, for the east prefer an arrival between 12:00 and 16:00. If that is not possible, accept a transition day: light in the local morning, no important decisions and a quiet evening. The Sfuso calculator can show you the effect of arrival time on your plan for the first days.

faq.q: Is it better to sleep or stay awake on an overnight flight?
faq.a: It depends on the time at your destination. If you land in the local morning, sleeping on the flight is an advantage because you arrive with more energy and can spend the day outdoors. Aim for real sleep, in the dark and without screens, rather than staying awake and crashing soon after arrival.

faq.q: Can I drink coffee before an overnight flight?
faq.a: Yes, but your last coffee should be at least 6 hours before the time you want to fall asleep, not before take-off. After that, stick to water or herbal teas. Caffeine stays in your system for a long time and makes sleep on the plane lighter, more fragmented and less restorative.

faq.q: How long can a nap on arrival last?
faq.a: At most 20-30 minutes, and not after 4pm local time. A longer or later rest risks taking away your sleep in the evening and slowing adjustment to the new time zone. Set an alarm so you do not go over, and then go straight out into natural light.

title: Jet lag on business trips: short or long, what to do
description: Jet lag on business trips: for trips of 1-3 days it is best to stay on home time, for longer ones you need to adjust. Here is how to decide.
h1: Jet lag on business trips: stay on home time or adjust?
intro: On short business trips of 1 to 3 days it is usually best to stay on home time rather than adjust to the time zone, whereas on longer trips it makes sense to shift your body clock. The choice depends on how many days you stay and when your commitments are. Here is a simple rule for deciding.

paragraphs: If you stay a short time, your body does not have time to adapt and would then have to do it all again on the way back. It is often more efficient to keep your home schedule: sleep and eat as if you were in the UK, even if local time is different.

An example: you leave for New York (5 hours behind the UK in winter) for two days. If at home you wake at 7, it would be 2 in the morning there. Keeping your own rhythm means meetings at a time that for your body is afternoon and evening, and sleep in the early hours of the local morning.
list: Keep your wake-up time and meals on home time as much as possible.
Concentrate important commitments in the hours when your body is most alert.
Avoid bright light in the hours when it would be night at home.
Use blackout curtains and an eye mask to sleep when you need to.

sections.h2: When it is better not to stay on home time
paragraphs: With very large time differences, for example Tokyo (+9 in winter) or Sydney (+11), staying on home time means being awake at night and asleep by day. If your meetings are in local office hours, it is not practicable.

In these cases you can choose a compromise: shift your times a little, but without chasing the full time difference. If you need to be at your best for an important meeting, arrive with a day to spare.

If you stay more than three or four days, adjusting is the best choice. Heading east you advance by about 1 hour a day, heading west you delay by about 1.5 hours a day; if you do nothing it takes about 1 day per hour of time difference.

You can prepare 1-3 days before by shifting sleep and wake-up by 1 hour a day. Once there, use light: in the hours after your body temperature minimum (about 2 hours before you usually wake up) it moves your clock earlier, in the hours before it moves it later. With the Sfuso calculator you can see the plan day by day.

If you travel often, choose flights arriving in the middle of the day if you go east (between 12:00 and 16:00 is ideal), while heading west it is best to arrive mid-day and stay outdoors until the evening. Do not schedule important meetings on the day of arrival if you can avoid it.
Watch your coffee and alcohol: your last coffee at least 6 hours before sleeping and no alcohol to get to sleep. If you are thinking about melatonin, talk to your doctor or pharmacist first.

Imagine leaving London for Tokyo (+9 in winter) for a week. That is 9 hours’ difference from the UK in winter, so it is worth adjusting: leave with 1-3 days of preparation, arrive the day before the main event and use the light of the local morning. For a two-day trip to New York, on the other hand, you stay on home time and put meetings in the hours when your body is awake.

The useful rule is to compare the days you stay with the hours of time difference. If the days are few compared with the hours, do not adjust. If the days are equal or more, adjust and use light and regular times.

faq.q: Do I need to adjust to the time zone for a two-day trip?
faq.a: Generally no. With a stay of 1-3 days the body does not have time to adapt, so it is best to stay on home time and schedule your commitments for the hours when you are most alert, taking care over light, meals and sleep as far as you can.

faq.q: After how many days is it worth adjusting to local time?
faq.a: As a general rule, beyond 3-4 days of stay it is worth adjusting. Heading east you advance by about 1 hour a day, heading west by about 1.5 hours a day, so with large time differences the process takes several days. The Sfuso calculator helps you estimate it.

faq.q: How do I prepare before a long business trip?
faq.a: In the 1-3 days before you leave, shift sleep and wake-up by about 1 hour a day in the direction of travel. Then aim for an arrival in the middle of the day and spend your time outdoors. The Sfuso calculator gives you a plan based on your usual wake-up time.

title: Melatonin and caffeine for jet lag: what to know
description: Melatonin and caffeine for jet lag: when they help, when they do not, and why you should always ask a doctor or pharmacist before using them.
h1: Melatonin and caffeine for jet lag: what to know
intro: Melatonin can help realign your sleep after a flight, especially heading east, while caffeine helps you stay awake but can make your night worse. Neither replaces light and regular times. Rules on melatonin vary from country to country, so ask a doctor or pharmacist before using it. You will not find doses here, only the general picture.

paragraphs: Melatonin is the hormone your body produces in the evening in the dark and that signals to your brain that it is time to sleep. Taking it as a supplement can help shift your body clock and fall asleep in the new time zone.

A Cochrane review (Herxheimer and Petrie, 2002) found that melatonin can reduce jet lag, with clearer effects on trips heading east and when crossing many time zones. It is not a magic solution: it helps, but on its own it is not enough.

sections.h2: When and how it makes sense to talk about it
paragraphs: In the first days, melatonin is taken at the time you want to fall asleep in the new time zone. Heading east, where you have to advance your clock, it is more useful; heading west it is needed less, because delaying is easier and your body adapts by about 1.5 hours a day.
How melatonin is sold and regulated differs from one country to another. For this reason it is always best to ask your doctor or pharmacist, especially in these cases:
list: children and teenagers
pregnancy and breastfeeding
taking other medicines, even over the counter
existing health problems or sleep disorders
driving or precision work soon after taking it

paragraphs: Caffeine keeps you awake, so it can help in the hours when you need to stay sharp after a flight. The problem is that it stays in your system for a long time: your last coffee should be at least 6 hours before the time you want to sleep.

If you arrive at your destination in the morning and are tired, a coffee can help. But if you drink it in the early local afternoon, you risk not falling asleep in the evening and slowing adjustment. Remember tea, cola and chocolate too, which contain caffeine.

Neither melatonin nor coffee shifts your body clock as much as light. Your lowest body temperature falls about 2 hours before you usually wake up: light in the hours after it moves your clock earlier, light in the hours before it moves it later. Use the Sfuso calculator to know when to seek or avoid the sun.
Add short naps, at most 20-30 minutes and not after 4pm local time, and meal times consistent with the new time zone. These are simple choices that often count for more than a supplement.

Do not take supplements just because a colleague or friend did: the response changes from person to person and also depends on when you take them. Avoid combining them with alcohol, which worsens sleep quality and makes you wake in the middle of the night.

If you notice morning drowsiness, headaches or new symptoms, stop and talk to a doctor. To decide whether and how to use melatonin, the right source is always a health professional who knows your situation.

faq.q: Does melatonin work against jet lag?
faq.a: A Cochrane review (Herxheimer and Petrie, 2002) indicates that it can help, especially on trips heading east, if taken at the time you want to fall asleep in the first days. It does not replace light and regular times, and it is best to check with a doctor or pharmacist first.

faq.q: When should I have my last coffee?
faq.a: At least 6 hours before the time you want to go to sleep in the new time zone. Caffeine stays in the body for a long time and can make it hard to fall asleep, slowing adjustment. After that time stick to water or herbal teas, and remember that tea and cola contain caffeine too.

faq.q: Can I give melatonin to a child?
faq.a: Do not do it on your own initiative. Rules on melatonin vary from country to country, and for children you need your paediatrician’s opinion. The same goes for pregnancy, breastfeeding or taking other medicines: always ask a doctor or pharmacist, without improvising doses.

title: Jet lag coming home to the UK: why it hits and what to do
description: Jet lag on coming home to the UK is often underestimated: how to get back in shape after a trip east or west, with light, routines and short naps.
h1: Jet lag coming home to the UK: the time shift you do not expect
intro: Jet lag on coming home to the UK is the mismatch you feel on returning home after adapting to the time zone of your trip, and it is often underestimated because it seems that at home everything goes back to normal at once. In reality your body clock has shifted and has to come back, at different rates depending on the direction.

paragraphs: During the trip you adapted, at least in part, to local time. Coming home you have to make the journey back in reverse. On top of that, you often return to a load of work, family and commitments that leave no time to recover.

If you went west, for example to Los Angeles (8 hours behind the UK in winter), on the way back you fly east and have to advance your clock: it is the harder direction, about 1 hour a day. If you went east, for example to Bangkok (+7) or Tokyo (+9), the return heading west is easier, at about 1.5 hours a day.
If you have time, start shifting sleep and wake-up by 1 hour a day in the 1-3 days before you return, in the direction of home. Even small shifts reduce the shock on arrival.

If you can, choose a flight that gets you in during the afternoon, particularly if you are coming back from the west: between 12:00 and 16:00 is the most comfortable time for the return heading east. Avoid planning important commitments for the day after you arrive.
list: Leave a free day on your return, when possible.
Sort out shopping or meals in advance.
Avoid coffee in the 6 hours before bed.
Take an eye mask and earplugs for the flight.

paragraphs: As soon as you arrive, go outdoors and seek light. Light in the hours after your body temperature minimum (about 2 hours before you usually wake up) moves your clock earlier; light in the hours before it moves it later. If you are coming back from the west, this helps you bring your wake-up back towards UK time.
Resist a long nap. If you really cannot manage, 20-30 minutes at most and not after 4pm local time. Go to bed at a reasonable time even if you are not very sleepy, and keep the bedroom dark.

sections.h2: How long it lasts and what to expect
paragraphs: If you do nothing, it takes about 1 day per hour of time difference. With light, regular times and consistent meals it gets shorter, but returning from large time differences can take a week or more.

If the time difference is very large heading east, for example over 9-10 hours, your body may find it more natural to delay than to advance. The Sfuso calculator takes this into account and gives you a day-by-day plan for the return too.

The most frequent is sleeping late on the first morning to recover: moving your wake-up later slows the return of your rhythm. It is better to get up at a reasonable time, go out into the light and take a short nap only if needed.
Another mistake is returning and going straight back to full speed. If you can, give yourself a buffer day, eat at regular times and do not drink coffee after midday in the first days.

faq.q: Is jet lag on the way back worse than on the way out?
faq.a: It depends on the direction. Coming back from west to east is usually more tiring because you have to advance your clock, about 1 hour a day. Coming back from east to west is easier, because your body delays by about 1.5 hours a day.

faq.q: How many days does it take to readjust to UK time?
faq.a: If you do nothing, about 1 day for every hour of time difference. If your trip had a 6-hour difference, it can take as much as a week. With light at the right moment, regular meals and short naps, the time shortens considerably.

faq.q: Can I work the day after I get back?
faq.a: You can, but it is best to avoid decisive commitments if the time difference is large. Planning a day to spare, going out into the light, eating at regular times and taking short naps, 20-30 minutes at most, helps you be sharper and find your rhythm again.

title: Light and jet lag: when to seek the sun and when to avoid it
description: How to use sunlight and sunglasses to shift your body clock and reduce jet lag: when to seek light, when to avoid it and how to time it day by day.
h1: Light and jet lag: how to shift your body clock with the sun
intro: Light is the most powerful signal for shifting your body clock: taken at the right moment it reduces jet lag, taken at the wrong moment it makes it worse. The reference is your lowest body temperature, which falls about 2 hours before you usually wake up. Light after that point moves your clock earlier, light before it moves it later.

paragraphs: Your body has a moment of the night when temperature reaches its minimum, about 2 hours before you usually wake up. If you wake at 7, it is around 5. It is the pivot around which everything turns.

Light in the hours after that point moves your clock earlier, that is it makes you feel sleepy sooner in the evening. Light in the hours before it moves your clock later, that is it makes you feel sleepy later. Knowing where you are in your cycle, hour by hour in the new time zone, is the key.

When you fly east, for example to Dubai (+4) or Tokyo (+9 in winter), you have to move earlier. You can shift your clock by about 1 hour a day. Seek light in the morning after your minimum and avoid evening light, which would delay you.

There are special cases: over 9-10 hours east, for example to Australia, it is often better to delay instead of advance. In that case evening light helps and morning light should be avoided in the first days. The Sfuso calculator tells you which strategy to follow.
list: Ideal arrival heading east: between 12:00 and 16:00.
On the first day, seek light in the afternoon, not too early.
In the following days, bring your light exposure forward by an hour.

paragraphs: Heading west, for example New York (−5) or Los Angeles (−8), you have to delay, and your body manages about 1.5 hours a day. Arrive in the middle of the day and stay outdoors until the evening: evening light helps you push your sleep later.
In the early morning, if you wake long before the local dawn, stay in dimly lit places. In this case light before your minimum would delay you, but if it comes too early it can confuse things.

Sunglasses are for avoiding light at the wrong hours. If you go out at a time when light would shift you in the opposite direction, wear them: they reduce the effect of the sun on your clock. In the evening, indoors, turn down the lights and limit screens.

Artificial light counts too, but much less than the sun outdoors. During the day, cloudy or not, an hour outside is more effective than staying in a lit room. A nap no later than 4pm local time and of 20-30 minutes at most avoids interfering with sleep.

If you usually wake at 7, the minimum falls around 5. Leaving the UK for New York (−5), 5 at home corresponds to midnight local time: evening light there delays you, which is what you want. Heading to Dubai (+4), 5 becomes 9 local time: light after that hour moves you earlier.

These calculations change every day, because your minimum shifts as you adapt. That is why the plan works day by day, not just once. The Sfuso calculator updates it for you, giving you light and dark windows every day.

faq.q: When should I seek light to move my body clock earlier?
faq.a: In the hours after your lowest body temperature, which falls about 2 hours before you usually wake up. Light in that window moves your clock earlier and makes you feel sleepy sooner in the evening. Avoid light in the hours before that point.

faq.q: Do sunglasses help against jet lag?
faq.a: Yes, if you use them to avoid light at the hours when it would shift you in the wrong direction, because they reduce the intensity reaching your eyes. They do not replace the right light at the right time, though, which remains the main and most effective tool against jet lag.

faq.q: Can artificial light replace the sun?
faq.a: It can help a little, but outdoors natural light is much more intense, even under cloud. To shift your body clock, it is better to spend time outside at the right hours and turn the lights down in the evening, limiting screens in the hours before bed.
